lectures.title: More on Gates + Superdense Coding
lectures.homework:
Resources

Superdense Coding (qiskit.org)

Homework

  • Completing superdense coding
    • As a reminder, the protocol is as follows
      • Alice and Bob share an epr pair |00> + |11> where Alice has the first qubit and Bob has the second qubit
      • Alice rolls a die and gets 0, 1, 2, 3 (which Bob now has to guess what she got)
      • Alice does the following depending on what she rolled
        • If she rolled a 0, she does nothing
        • If she rolled a 1, she applies the X gate
        • If she rolled a 2, she applies the Z gate
        • If she rolled a 3, she applies the Y gate
      • Alice then sends her qubit over to Bob
      • Bob has both qubits. He applies the CNOT gate and then H gate to the first qubit
      • Bob then measures both qubits
    • Homework: Show that Bob gets a different result for both measurements depending on whether Alice rolled a 0, 1, 2, 3.
  • Represent H with pauli matrices
  • What does XX, YY, ZZ do to a qubit?
    • e.g applying X on a qubit then applying X again.
    • Hint you can multiply the matrices to see what the final resulting matrix would do
  • What is the resulting 4x4 matrix when computing: X Ⓧ I (Pauli X matrix tensor product Identity Matrix)
  • For the motivated
    • (If you don’t do this don’t worry we will do it together next lecture) Write the complete superdense coding circuit in qiskit (as illustrated in lecture)
      • Function should take 2 classicals bit and would finally output 2 qubits that when measured would give |00>,|01>,|10>,|11> depending on the 2 input classical bits
    • For the very very motivated
      • Do superdense coding with a different shared epr pair (|01> + |10>)
  • Represent |++> state in vector form (in the 1x4 vector)

    • Deutsch-Jozsa
      • Show that H^n |0>^n = | i > (e.g demonstrate the equality with n=3)
        • Note how H^n |0>^n = |+>^n

        • We will be covering all of this in the class

    • Notes
      • 1. No operations will be performed on D throughout the protocol.
      • 2. Note how this is simply the quantum teleportation circuit we talked about in the lecture, except that C is entangled with D
    • Write the bell states in vector form and show that they are orthogonal.
      • For the very motivated, show that they form an orthogonal basis. An orthogonal basis means every other vector can be generated from these 4 and the states are orthogonal.

lectures.title: CHSH inequality
lectures.homework:
• In class, we went over Bell’s inequality and provided an example of a QM mechanical state and a set of measurements that violate Bell’s inequality. Since Bell’s paper, there have been other variants that have emerged. One such variant is the CHSH inequality.
    • Try to understand what the CHSH inequality is. Here are some resources: https://qiskit.org/textbook/ch-demos/chsh.html, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell%27s_theorem, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CHSH_inequality
    • What is the upper bound on the inequality classical?
    • What is an example of a quantum system that violates this upper bound?
    • For the motivated:
      • Can you prove the upper bound on the CHSH inequality?
      • (From Qiskit but many sources have this problem): Consider a game where Alice and Bob are put in separate rooms and each is given a bit x and y. respectively. These bits are chosen at random and independently of each other. On receiving the bit each of them replies with a bit of their own, a and b. Now, Alice and Bob win the game if a and b are different whenever x = y = 1 and equal otherwise. It is easy to see that the best possible strategy for Alice and Bob is to always give a = b = 0 (or 1). With this strategy, Alice and Bob can win the game at most 75% of the time. Imagine Alice and Bob are allowed to share an entangled two-qubit state. Is there a strategy they can use that would give them a better chance of winning than 75%? Remember that they can agree upon any strategy beforehand, but once they are given the random bits they cannot communicate anymore. They can take their respective parts of the entangled pair with them at all times, of course.)
  • We are going to talk about measurements in the next lecture. Here is a good resource to get you started if you are interested in reading ahead: https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs191/fa14/lectures/lecture89.pdf.

lectures.title: Stabilizer Codes
lectures.homework:
Resources

chap7.dvi (caltech.edu)

https://courses.cs.washington.edu/courses/cse599d/06wi/lecturenotes18.pdf

Homework

  1. Prove that Tr(M1 tensor M2) = Tr(M1) Tr(M2) (for any matrices M1, M2)
  2. Why is 𝐼 always in a stabilizer group? But why isn’t it in the generator of the group?
    1. 𝐼 is always in the stabilizer group because the inverse of each element exists in the group (by the definition of a group, see number 4)
    2. 𝐼 is not in the generator of the group because it can always be generated using a different generator element A and its inverse A-1. Note that A-1 is generated using A.
  3. Why can’t -𝐼 be in a stabilizer group?
    1. If -𝐼 is in a stabilizer group, then nothing can be in the +1 eigenspace since -𝐼|Ψ> = -|Ψ>
  4. [Optional Review]
    1. The overarching question of the lecture is:
      1. How do we define the conditions when it’s possible to correct errors?
        1. What errors can we tolerate?
      2. How many qubits do we need to represent one logical qubit?
      3. How do we encode our logical qubit to the stabilizer code?
      4. How do we apply logical operations on our codespace instead of decoding and re-encoding our state between operations?
      5. How do we eventually detect and correct the error?
    2. Terminology
      1. Subspace: A subset of a vector space that also satisfies the criteria of a vector space (closed under addition)
      2. Code Subspace: A subspace of the Hilbert space whose elements are in the +1 eigenspace of all the stabilizer group elements. (Note an element of the Hilbert space or the code subspace is a quantum state).
        1. In other words: the code subspace is the set of “valid” error-free encoded states for our stabilizer code.
      3. Code word: An element (state) within the code subspace.
      4. Stabilizer: A Pauli operator that helps us define our code subspace.
        1. Criteria: All stabilizers must commute with each other, and -𝐼 can’t be a stabilizer.
      5. Stabilizer Generator: The set of generators of the stabilizer group.
      6. Stabilizer Group: The group that’s generated by multiplying all combinations of the stabilizer generator.

lectures.homework:
1. Why do all stabilizers commute?
    1. They are all Pauli matrices, which either commute or anti-commute. SiSj|Ψ>=Si|Ψ>=|Ψ>=Si|Ψ>=SjSi|Ψ>
  2. What’s the difference between the stabilizers and the stabilizer generators?
    1. Stabilizer generators generate the whole stabilizer group (by multiplying them by each other)
  3. Prove that the trace of any matrix is the sum of its eigenvalues
    1. Solution
  4. Show that this control-Pauli circuit can be used to measure if |Ψ> is in the +1 or -1 eigenspace of the Pauli operator P (note that |Ψ> describes the state of n qubits)
    1. It can also be used for the preparation of +1, -1 states.
  5. Add a specific example here like the C-ZZZZZ to prepare a general state
  6. Topics to be covered next lecture
    1. Do the stabilizer elements need to commute?
    2. How many normalizer elements do we get?
    3. Quotient groups
    4. Preparations of stabilizer states using the C-Pauli circuits
    5. Universal X and Z gate?
  7. Review
    1. We define the Projector Pi = ½ (I + Si) -> projects us into the +1 eigenvalue subspace of S1 [Takes a minute to prove]
    2. Tr(Pi Sj) = 0 Proof: Tr(½ Sj + ½ Si Sj) = ½ Tr(Sj) + ½ Tr(Si Sj) = 0 + 0
      1. Sj is a pauli matrix so Tr(Sj) = 0
      2. Si Sj will give us another element in S which also have Trace 0
    3. Remember that Si splits our code space into two 2^(n-1) eigenspaces, +1 and -1
    4. Si and Sj divide our code space into 4 2^(n-1) eigenspaces, (+1,+1), (-1,+1), (+1,-1), (-1,-1)
    5. Normalizers N of a group S are elements P such that Ps=sP (where P ∈ Pn and s ∈ S)
      1. N/P (i.e., elements of P that are not stabilizers) can be treated as logical Pauli operators.
      2. Note that P|Ψ>=PS|Ψ>=SP|Ψ>
        1. Let P|Ψ> = |Φ>
        2. |Φ> = PS|Ψ>=S|Φ>
        3. Then S|Φ>=|Φ> so |Φ> is a code word (i.e, it has a +1 eigenvalue for our stabilizer group)
        4. E.g XXX|000> = |111> for the ZZI, ZIZ stabilizer group
      3. Elements of a normalizer group represent different operators on our encoded space
    6. If you want to implement any (logical) single qubit gate. You just need to implement a (logical) X gate and a (logical) Z gate, and you are done.
    7. For example, for the ZZI, ZIZ stabilizer generators
      1. N-S = ik(XXX, YYX, YXY, YXX, …)

          1. This hilbert space has a dimension of 2N

Final Homework!!!!!

Your Final HW will be to understand a new quantum computing algorithm or topic and explain it to us in a lecture.

FAQs

  • How do I find a quantum algorithm?
    • There is a big list of quantum algorithms here: https://quantumalgorithmzoo.org/
    • You can find more here: List of Open Quantum Projects (qosf.org)
    • Even more here: Quantum Algorithm Implementations for Beginners (arxiv.org)
    • If this list seems overwhelming, ask us and we can suggest you a handful
  • What are some other topics:
    • Draper Adder
      • DraperQFTAdder — Qiskit 0.34.2 documentation
      • original paper
    • QRAM:
      • Primer (there are many different implementations that are more involved than this)
      • Implementing QRAM in Qiskit with code — Quantum Computing UK
    • Quantum algorithms (CO 781): Final project (uwaterloo.ca)
    • CS667/CO681/PH767 Potential Project Topics (uwaterloo.ca)
    • QRAM: 0708.1879.pdf (arxiv.org)
    • How do D-Wave computers work (look into QUBO problems)?
      • You can try reading this book
    • QAOA
      • TSP
      • Max-Cut problem: uses  MinimumEigenOptimizer in combination of QAOA  as minimum eigensolver routine.
      • Variational Quantum Algorithms
    • Quantum Machine Learning (look up NISQ)
      • Qiskit ML
        • https://github.com/Qiskit/qiskit-machine-learning/
        • https://qiskit.org/documentation/machine-learning/tutorials/index.html
    • Qiskit Finance: Finance Tutorials — Qiskit Finance 0.3.1 documentation
    • Quantum Error Correction (Steane Code, Bacon-Shor Codes, Hamming Codes, etc.)
    • Topological Quantum Computing
    • Quantum Cryptography
      • Algebraic attacks on block ciphers using quantum annealing (turning the problem into a QUBO)
    • Threads asking about project ideas
      • https://quantumcomputing.stackexchange.com/questions/8481/ideas-for-school-level-project-on-quantum-computing
      • https://quantumcomputing.stackexchange.com/questions/4420/algorithm-based-game-project-to-introduce-quantum-computing
      • https://quantumcomputing.stackexchange.com/questions/8290/newbie-project-calculate-a-mersenne-prime-with-quantum-computing
    • Approximate cloning
  • There are too many topics! How do I pick one?
    • Try to pick something that’s relatively easy (but not too easy). So at least you can understand the problem within a few hours of reading the problem statement.
    • Try to pick something that’s exciting so you can push through understanding both the problem and the algorithm until the end.
      • For example: If you like cryptography you might want to read about Shor’s solution for the discrete logarithm problem that allows us to break Diffie-Helman exchange
    • You can try to optimize for a problem in a group of problems that spans too many more algorithms, this way your acquired knowledge can go a long way.
      • For example the Hidden subgroup problem spans a lot of problems (Simon’s, Grover’s, Shor’s are all instance of the Abelian hidden subgroup problem)
  • What resources can help me?
    • Wikipedia is always useful resource
    • Qiskit may not have the exact algorithm you are looking for but it has nice explanations for concepts that will allow you to understand the problem/solution.
    • Quantum Computing and Quantum Information book
    • Lectures on youtube
  • Can we ask for help?
    • Yes come to office hours and we will try to help

syllabus:
1. Intro to qubits
  2. Vectors and Matrices
  3. Superdense coding
  4. Quantum Teleportation
  5. Deutsch (Find whether a function is constant or balanced in O(1) vs O(2^(n-1)) classically)
  6. Simon's Algorithm (how to find xor pairs in O(n), where classically it's O(2^n/2))
  7. EPR Pair and Bell’s Inequality (Bell showing us why Einstein is wrong)
  8. Grover's (Search in O(sqrt(N)))
    1. [5,1,4,9….] N
    2. Search: O(N)
    3. Quantum Computing: O(sqrt(N))
  9. Measurement
  10. No cloning theorem (Why copying qubits is impossible!)
    1. Quantum circuits and universal quantum gates
  11. Grover’s example oracles (qiskit code)
  12. RSA and Shor's Algorithm (Breaking RSA in logN polynomial time!)
    1. Period Finding
    2. QFT
    3. Factoring using period finding
  13. Hidden Subgroup Problem
    1. Phase Estimation/Continued Fractions
    2. Order Finding
    3. HSP problem definition + quantum algorithm
  14. How do quantum computers work physically?
    1. PreReqs:
      1. LC Circuits + DRAM
      2. Hamiltonians (will be useful for us later when we discuss AQC/QAOA/QA)
      3. Quantum Harmonic Oscillator
      4. Daniel’s thesis

    1. MaxCut
    2. TSP
    3. Algebraic attacks on block ciphers using quantum annealing (turning the problem into a QUBO)
  17. HHL/QRam
    1. HHL implementation (Qiskit Aqua has it)
  18. Quantum Error Correction
    1. Toric Code
    2. Shor’s Code
  19. Quantum Cryptography
    1. Quantum Key Distribution:
      1. BB84
        1. Implementation
  20. Quantum Counting
